title: Take-home Exercise 1: Geospatial Analytics for Public Safety
text:
8 Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
This section conducts an Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) to visualise the distribution of road accidents in the BMR in 2022. The findings identified will support the public safety discussion by providing relevant evidence about accident circumstances.

8.1 Overview Map

tm_shape(adm2_bmr) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "province_name", fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Province", na.show = FALSE)) +
tm_shape(roads_bmr) +
  tm_lines(col = "darkgreen", lwd = 1) +
tm_shape(accidents_bmr) +
  tm_dots(fill = "red", size = 0.05) +
tm_layout(main.title = "Road Traffic Accidents in the BMR (2022)", main.title.position = "center")














Note



Analysis:

Accident points are concentrated along the road network across the BMR, rather than scattered away from mapped roads.
Accident density appears visibly higher in the central portion of the study area, spanning parts of Bangkok, Nonthaburi, and Samut Prakan, compared to the northern part of Pathum Thani and the western part of Nakhon Pathom.
The road network itself appears denser in the central and southern portions of the study area, with a comparatively sparser network in the northern part of Pathum Thani.





8.2 Accidents by Month and Season
Accident counts are aggregated by month_label and season, highlighting how many accidents happen each month.

accidents_by_month <- accidents_bmr %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  count(month_label, season)

The result is plotted as a grouped bar chart using plotly.

plot_ly(accidents_by_month, x = ~month_label, y = ~n, color = ~season,
        colors = c("Cool" = "lightblue", "Hot" = "red3", "Rainy" = "royalblue3"),
        type = "bar") %>%
  layout(title = "Accidents by Month, Coloured by Season",
         xaxis = list(title = "Month"), yaxis = list(title = "Number of Accidents"),
         barmode = "stack")











Note



Analysis:

October, November, and December (Cool season) show the highest total accidents of the year, with October being the highest.
April (Hot season) also shows a high total accident count, standing out clearly above the other Hot season months.
February show comparatively lower total accidents than most other months.
The Rainy season months (June to September) show generally high and relatively consistent total accidents across that stretch, without a sharp peak or dip within the season.
The Hot season (mid-February to mid-May) shows more variation in total accidents between its months than the Rainy or Cool seasons, ranging from one of the lowest totals (February) to one of the highest (April).




8.2.1 Event: Songkran Festival
This subsection examines the impact of the Songkran festival on road accidents in April, a period known for increased travel and correspondingly elevated road risk. songkran_dangerous_days, derived in Feature Engineering, flags accidents falling within the 11 to 17 April Seven Dangerous Days window. Since this period covers 7 days against 23 remaining days in April, the average daily accident rate is compared rather than raw totals, to avoid a comparison biased toward whichever side has more days.

songkran_comparison <- accidents_bmr %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(month == 4) %>%
  count(songkran_dangerous_days) %>%
  mutate(
    days_count = if_else(songkran_dangerous_days, 7, 30 - 7),
    average_daily_accidents = n / days_count,
    label = if_else(songkran_dangerous_days, "Songkran (11 to 17 Apr)", "Rest of April")
  )

plot_ly(songkran_comparison, x = ~label, y = ~average_daily_accidents, color = ~label,
        colors = c("Songkran (11 to 17 Apr)" = "tomato1", "Rest of April" = "royalblue3"),
        type = "bar") %>%
  layout(title = "Average Daily Accident Rate: Songkran vs Rest of April",
         xaxis = list(title = "Period"), yaxis = list(title = "Average Accidents per Day"),
         showlegend = FALSE)











Note



Analysis:

The average daily accident rate during the Songkran Seven Dangerous Days (11 to 17 April) is substantially higher than the average daily rate for the rest of April, more than double.
This is consistent with Songkran being a period of nationally elevated road risk, attributed to the surge in travel during the holiday.






8.3 Accidents by Day of Week
Instead of just analysing based on individual day, accidents are split by weekday versus weekend.

accidents_by_day <- accidents_bmr %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  mutate(day_type = if_else(day_of_week %in% c("Sat", "Sun"), "Weekend", "Weekday")) %>%
  count(day_of_week, day_type)

plot_ly(accidents_by_day, x = ~day_of_week, y = ~n, color = ~day_type,
        colors = c("Weekday" = "orange", "Weekend" = "seagreen"), type = "bar") %>%
  layout(title = "Accidents by Day of Week",
         xaxis = list(title = "Day of Week"), yaxis = list(title = "Number of Accidents"))











Note



Analysis:

Weekday totals rise steadily across the week, from the lowest point on Tuesday to the highest point on Friday.
Between the two weekend days, Saturday records a noticeably higher total than Sunday.
Friday and Saturday together stand out as the two highest days overall, straddling the weekday to weekend transition. This may reflect increased travel for social or leisure purposes as the weekend begins.
Sunday’s accident drop back toward weekday levels could reflect reduced travel activity as the weekend winds down.





8.4 Accidents by Peak Period
Accidents are examined by peak period: Morning Peak, Evening Peak, and Off-Peak.

accidents_by_peak <- accidents_bmr %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  count(peak_period) %>%
  mutate(
    peak_period = factor(peak_period, levels = c("Morning Peak", "Evening Peak", "Off-Peak")),
    hours_in_period = case_when(
      peak_period == "Morning Peak" ~ 2,
      peak_period == "Evening Peak" ~ 3,
      peak_period == "Off-Peak" ~ 19
    ),
    accidents_per_hour = n / hours_in_period
  )

plot_ly(accidents_by_peak, x = ~peak_period, y = ~accidents_per_hour, type = "bar",
        marker = list(color = c("Morning Peak" = "orange", "Evening Peak" = "tomato", "Off-Peak" = "lightblue")[as.character(accidents_by_peak$peak_period)])) %>%
  layout(title = "Average Accidents per Hour by Peak Period",
         xaxis = list(title = "Peak Period", categoryorder = "array", categoryarray = c("Morning Peak", "Evening Peak", "Off-Peak")),
         yaxis = list(title = "Accidents per Hour"))











Important



Morning Peak, Evening Peak, and Off-Peak are unequal length periods: 2, 3, and 19 hours respectively. A raw count comparison across peak_period would favour Off-Peak simply because it covers more clock time, instead of carrying more risk per hour. Counts are therefore converted to an average per hour before comparison, so that the three periods are placed on equal footing.








Note



Analysis:

Morning Peak records the highest average accidents per hour among the three periods, narrowly ahead of Evening Peak.
Both Morning and Evening Peak records are well above Off-Peak. Off-Peak records the lowest average accidents per hour.





8.5 Accidents by Presumed Cause
The presumed cause recorded for each accident is counted and ranked.

accidents_bmr %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  count(presumed_cause, sort = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(presumed_cause = fct_reorder(presumed_cause, n)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = presumed_cause)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Accidents by Presumed Cause", x = "Number of Accidents", y = NULL)














Note



Analysis:

Speeding is the most common presumed cause, well ahead of every other category. It accounts for a substantially larger number of accidents than every other category combined.
All other causes account for comparatively few accidents each, with a long tail of rarely recorded categories.





8.6 Accidents by Accident Type
Accidents are broken down by accident type.

accidents_bmr %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  count(accident_type, sort = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(accident_type = fct_reorder(accident_type, n)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = accident_type)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Accidents by Accident Type", x = "Number of Accidents", y = NULL)














Note



Analysis:

Rear-end collision is the most common accident type, followed by rollover/fallen on straight road.
The remaining types account for a comparatively smaller number of accidents.





8.7 Accidents by Vehicle Type
vehicle_type contains a long tail of rare categories. Only the ten most frequent are shown.

accidents_bmr %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  count(vehicle_type, sort = TRUE) %>%
  slice_max(n, n = 10) %>%
  mutate(vehicle_type = fct_reorder(vehicle_type, n)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = vehicle_type)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Top 10 Vehicle Types Involved in Accidents", x = "Number of Accidents", y = NULL)














Note



Analysis:

Private/passenger car and 4-wheel pickup truck are the two most common vehicle types involved.
The remaining vehicle types account for a comparatively small share of the top ten.





8.8 Accidents by Weather Condition
The weather condition recorded at the time of each accident is broken down by category.

accidents_bmr %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  count(weather_condition, sort = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(weather_condition = fct_reorder(weather_condition, n)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = weather_condition)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Accidents by Weather Condition", x = "Number of Accidents", y = NULL)














Note



Analysis:

The majority of accidents occurred under clear weather conditions.
Rainy conditions account for a much smaller share of accidents.





8.9 Overall Severity
Total accidents, fatalities, injuries, and the count of accidents involving at least one fatality are summarised below.

accidents_bmr %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  summarise(
    total_accidents = n(),
    total_fatalities = sum(number_of_fatalities),
    total_injuries = sum(number_of_injuries),
    fatal_accidents = sum(number_of_fatalities > 0)
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 4
  total_accidents total_fatalities total_injuries fatal_accidents
            <int>            <dbl>          <dbl>           <int>
1            3593              176           2093             159

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Geospatial Analytics for Public Safety
text:
10 Spatio-Temporal Point Pattern Analysis

10.1 Spatio-Temporal KDE by Month
KDE and quadrat analysis above addressed how accident intensity varies across space. This section focuses on the temporal portion, examining whether accident intensity varies across the year. The point pattern is split by month, and a separate density surface is computed for each.

accidents_ppp_month <- accidents_ppp_km
marks(accidents_ppp_month) <- marks(accidents_ppp_km)$month

st_kde <- spattemp.density(accidents_ppp_month)
summary(st_kde)

Spatiotemporal Kernel Density Estimate

Bandwidths
  h = 4.8825 (spatial)
  lambda = 0.0285 (temporal)

No. of observations
  3593 

Spatial bound
  Type: polygonal
  2D enclosure: [565.5458, 743.0603] x [1468.71, 1599.777]

Temporal bound
  [1, 12]

Evaluation
  128 x 128 x 12 trivariate lattice
  Density range: [7.546022e-35, 0.002849939]


Twelve monthly slices are plotted on a shared colour scale for direct comparison across the year:

par(mfrow = c(4, 3), mar = c(2, 2, 2, 2))
for (i in 1:12) {
  plot(st_kde, i,
       override.par = FALSE,
       fix.range = TRUE,
       main = paste("Month", i))
}














Note



Analysis:
Month 1 shows a moderately widespread hotspot concentrated in the central BMR, with some diffusion into surrounding areas.
Months 2 to 7 show generally lower intensity, with hotspots more contained.
Months 8 to 11 show accident density concentrated around Bangkok increasing in both intensity and spatial extent, with the branching pattern along major roads becoming more pronounced.
Month 12 shows the highest density of the year, concentrated in central BMR, likely due to increased travel during the year-end and holiday period. This also coincides with the start of Thailand’s New Year “Seven Dangerous Days” period, 29 December 2022 to 4 January 2023, of which 29 to 31 December falls within the study period. 317 deaths were recorded nationwide GT Rider, citing Thailand’s Road Safety Centre, 2023.
